name: Battle of Fotevik
location: Fotevik, a shallow bay on the Scanian coast south of Malmö
summary: The battle of 4 June 1134 in which Eric II destroyed the army of his uncle King Niels on the Scanian shore, killed Niels’s son Magnus the Strong, and took the Danish crown. Five bishops died fighting on the royal side, the heaviest loss the Danish church ever suffered in a single day.
details: Eric Emune had been beaten repeatedly since raising his revolt to avenge the murder of Canute Lavard in 1131. At Fotevik he fought with the Scanians behind him, the archbishop of Lund’s blessing, and a force of German mailed horsemen hired from Holstein. Niels landed his army from the fleet into the bay and was ridden down. Magnus the Strong was killed, the old king escaped, and three weeks later the guildsmen of Schleswig cut him down in the town of the duke his son had murdered.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: On 4 June 1134 the army of King Niels of Denmark was destroyed at Fotevik, a bay on the Scanian coast below the Falsterbo peninsula. The victor was his nephew Eric, called Emune, who had spent three years losing battles to him. The dead included Niels’s son and co-king Magnus the Strong, the man whose killing of Canute Lavard in 1131 had begun the war.

What makes Fotevik unusual is the casualty list. Five Danish bishops were killed on the royal side, along with a large number of priests, because the church of Jutland and the islands had gone to war with its king’s army in person. Nothing comparable happened again in medieval Denmark, and the loss is the single fact about the battle that every medieval source records.

The battle also marks the arrival of a new kind of fighting in the north. Eric had hired German heavy cavalry, and the Danish sources treat their charge as the thing that decided the day. Within a generation the Danish crown was raising its own mailed horsemen, and the levy of ships and axes that had fought Denmark’s wars for two centuries began to give way.

contentSections.title: The murder at Haraldsted
paragraphs: Niels had ruled since 1104, the last of the sons of Sweyn Estridsen to hold the throne, and by the 1120s the succession was a problem with two answers. His son Magnus expected it. So did Canute Lavard, son of the previous king Eric I, whom Niels had made duke in Schleswig and who had taken the title of king of the Obotrites from the German emperor — a Danish prince holding a crown of his own on the southern border.

On 7 January 1131 Magnus lured Canute into the woods at Haraldsted near Ringsted, on the pretext of a private talk, and killed him. The killing of a kinsman under a safe-conduct offended in a way an ordinary dynastic murder did not, and Canute’s reputation as a just and popular lord made it worse. He was canonised in 1170 and the church at Ringsted became his shrine.

Canute’s half-brother Eric took up the feud at once. The first three years went badly for him: he was beaten in Jutland and at Onsild and Vaerebro, and he fled to Norway and then to Scania. What changed was not his generalship but who was willing to fund it.

contentSections.title: Scania, Lund, and the German horse
paragraphs: Scania was the richest of the Danish provinces and the seat of the archbishopric of Lund, which since 1104 had held the primacy over all Scandinavia. Niels had allowed that primacy to be questioned, and Archbishop Asser had reason to want a king who would defend it. Scania declared for Eric, and it was from Scania that he fought the last campaign.

Eric also bought help abroad. He obtained a force of mailed German horsemen from Holstein, professional cavalry of a sort Denmark did not yet field, and brought them across to the Scanian shore. Saxo and the Danish chronicles agree that this contingent was small and that it was decisive, which is the combination that makes an account credible: nobody exaggerating a victory invents a foreign minority and gives it the credit.

Niels answered by bringing his army to Scania by sea, the ordinary Danish way of moving an army, and landing it at Fotevik. The bay is shallow and open, and putting a levy ashore from ships into open ground in front of waiting cavalry is close to the worst position such a force can be given.

contentSections.title: The battle
paragraphs: No source describes the fighting in any detail. What the Danish annals and Saxo agree on is the outcome and its speed: the royal army broke soon after it was engaged, the German horse rode through it, and the killing happened as the levy tried to get back to the ships across open shore and shallow water.

Magnus the Strong was killed. So were five bishops, among them the bishop of Roskilde, and the chronicles put the number of priests who died with them at about sixty. The medieval lists of the fallen bishops do not entirely agree with one another, so the individual names are less secure than the number, which every account gives as five.

The presence of a bishops’ contingent on a battlefield needs no special explanation in twelfth-century Denmark, where a bishop held land and men and owed service for them. What Fotevik shows is the cost when the whole episcopate of one faction is present at a rout: there was no orderly withdrawal, and prelates in mail who could not run died with everyone else.

contentSections.title: Niels at Schleswig
paragraphs: Niels got off the field and away by ship. He made for Schleswig, which was a strange choice, because Schleswig was the town of the duke his son had murdered, and its merchant guild had honoured Canute Lavard as its patron.

On 25 June 1134, three weeks after the battle, the guildsmen of Schleswig fell on the king in the town and killed him. He was about sixty-nine, had reigned for thirty years, and was the last of the sons of Sweyn Estridsen; his death closed a run of five brothers on the Danish throne.

Eric was crowned as Eric II. He was king for barely three years and used them ruthlessly: his half-brother Harald Kesja, who had been raised up as a rival king in Jutland, was hunted down and killed in 1135 with most of his sons. On 18 September 1137 a magnate named Sorte Plov — Black Plough — ran Eric through with a spear at a public assembly near Ribe, in front of the whole gathering.

contentSections.title: What Fotevik settled and what it did not
paragraphs: Fotevik decided which branch of the family would rule, and nothing else. The war it ended was the first round of a Danish civil conflict that ran, with pauses, for twenty-three more years: Eric II was murdered in 1137, his nephew Eric III abdicated in 1146, and the kingdom then split three ways between Sweyn III, Canute V and Valdemar. It closed only at Grathe Heath in 1157.

The long-term winner was Canute Lavard’s line. His posthumous son was the Valdemar who survived the Bloodfeast of Roskilde and became Valdemar I, and the Valdemarian kings who made Denmark a Baltic power in the later twelfth century descended from the duke murdered at Haraldsted, not from either of the men who fought at Fotevik.

At the bay itself, underwater survey has found a barrier of deliberately sunken ships across the approaches at Fotevik, of a kind used to close a harbour against attack. Its dating has been associated with this period and the battle, though a blockade is a standing defence rather than a battlefield feature, and it should not be read as part of the fighting of 4 June.

leaders.name: Archbishop Asser of Lund
leaders.title: Archbishop Asser of Lund
leaders.note: First archbishop of Lund and the churchman whose province backed Eric. No Codex article yet: he belongs to the history of the Scandinavian primacy rather than to this battlefield, and the sources place him behind the revolt rather than in the line.

strength.display: Unknown; a Scanian levy stiffened by a few hundred German mailed horsemen
strength.note: No source counts either army. The Danish accounts agree only that the hired German cavalry were a small part of Eric’s force and the part that broke the royal army.

participants.side: The royal army of King Niels

leaders.name: Magnus the Strong
leaders.title: Magnus the Strong
leaders.note: Niels’s son and co-king, who had murdered Canute Lavard in 1131 and was killed in this battle. No Codex article: he is recorded almost entirely through that killing and this defeat.

strength.display: Unknown; a ship-borne royal levy landed into the bay
strength.note: Medieval accounts record the dead rather than the numbers engaged. The five bishops and about sixty priests killed are the only figures any source gives.

outcome: Decisive victory for Eric Emune. Magnus the Strong and five Danish bishops were killed, the royal army was destroyed, and King Niels escaped only to be killed by the guildsmen of Schleswig on 25 June 1134. Eric took the throne as Eric II.

imageInfo.caption: Fotevik in Scania, the shallow bay where King Niels landed his army in June 1134, in an aerial photograph by the archaeologist Sven Rosborn.
imageInfo.creator: Sven Rosborn
imageInfo.date: Modern aerial photograph; the battle was fought on 4 June 1134
imageInfo.note: A photograph of the ground, not of the battle: no depiction of Fotevik survives from any period, and the Danish, Swedish and English encyclopedia articles all lead with this same view for that reason. It shows the shallow open water and low shore that made a landing here so costly, and it is under this bay that a barrier of deliberately sunken ships was found. Released into the public domain by the photographer.

battleContinuity.label: Where the Danish civil wars ended
battleContinuity.reason: Fotevik settled which branch of Sweyn Estridsen’s family would rule and nothing more; the fighting went on through three more reigns until Valdemar destroyed Sweyn III at Grathe Heath in 1157 and reunited the kingdom under the line of the duke whose murder had started it.

people.title: Valdemar I of Denmark
people.label: Posthumous son of the murdered Canute Lavard

events.title: Battle of Grathe Heath
events.label: The battle that ended the same civil wars in 1157

locations.title: Roskilde
locations.label: Its bishop was among the five who died here

houses.title: House of Estridsen
houses.label: Both armies were led by men of this house

sources.title: Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum
sources.author: Saxo Grammaticus, about 1200
sources.note: The fullest narrative of the war, written two generations later under the patronage of the winning line.

timeline.title: Niels becomes king
timeline.description: The youngest son of Sweyn Estridsen takes the throne after his brother Eric I dies on pilgrimage, and rules for thirty years.

timeline.title: Canute Lavard made duke
timeline.description: Niels gives his nephew the border duchy of Schleswig, where he builds a following and takes a crown of his own among the Obotrites.

timeline.title: Murder at Haraldsted
timeline.description: Magnus the Strong kills Canute Lavard in the woods near Ringsted under a safe-conduct, and the Danish civil wars begin.

timeline.title: Eric beaten repeatedly
timeline.description: Canute’s half-brother Eric loses his early battles against the king, is driven out of Jutland and takes refuge in Norway and then Scania.

timeline.title: Scania and Lund declare for Eric
timeline.description: The richest Danish province and the archbishopric that held the Scandinavian primacy back the pretender against the king.

timeline.title: Fotevik
timeline.description: Niels’s army is landed into the bay and broken by Eric’s hired German horse. Magnus the Strong dies with five bishops and about sixty priests.

timeline.title: Niels killed at Schleswig
timeline.description: The old king flees to the town of the duke his son had murdered, and its guildsmen kill him there.

timeline.title: Harald Kesja destroyed
timeline.description: Eric II hunts down the half-brother who had been raised as a rival king in Jutland and kills him with most of his sons.

timeline.title: Eric II murdered
timeline.description: A magnate called Sorte Plov spears the king at a public assembly near Ribe, and the crown passes to his nephew Eric III.

timeline.title: The wars end
timeline.description: After three-way partition and the Bloodfeast of Roskilde, Valdemar destroys Sweyn III at Grathe Heath and reunites the kingdom.

timeline.title: Canute Lavard canonised
timeline.description: The duke murdered at Haraldsted is made a saint at Ringsted, where his son Valdemar I has his own heir crowned co-king on the same day.
